common_name: Can Can Scarlet Carnation (AAS and Fleuroselect Award-Winning Hardy Garden Carnation)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter and set out hardened transplants around the last frost date, or sow directly once soil has warmed.

directions: Sow indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost or direct-sow after soil has warmed, then plant out in sharply drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Can Can Scarlet is a hardy, heat-tolerant garden carnation bred for an F1 trial-winning strain, producing fully double, fringed scarlet-red blooms with an intensely spicy clove fragrance over a long summer season. Deadhead spent stems regularly to keep flowering flushing from early summer into fall, and avoid overly rich or soggy soil, which encourages rot and weak stems. It performs well both as a garden perennial and as a cut flower.

common_name: Enfant de Nice Carnation (French Heirloom Fragrant Mixed-Color Carnation)

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late winter for bloom the first summer, since this strain flowers slowly from seed; in mild climates it can also be treated as a short-lived perennial or biennial.

directions: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and transplant into lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun once danger of frost has passed. Enfant de Nice is an old French carnation strain grown for cutting, producing fully double blooms in a mix of scarlet, pink, and white, many with striped or picotee markings, on strong stems with an intense clove scent. Pinch young plants to encourage branching and stake taller stems if grown for cut flowers, and deadhead to extend the summer bloom season. It is best treated as an annual or short-lived perennial where winters are cold and wet.

common_name: Fruit Punch Whipped Cream Dianthus (Proven Winners Double White Fragrant Interspecific Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full to part sun; Whipped Cream is part of the Proven Winners Fruit Punch series bred for improved heat tolerance and repeat bloom.

directions: Plant divisions or container plants in very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full to part sun. Whipped Cream, part of the Proven Winners Fruit Punch series, produces abundant double, pure-white flowers with fuller petals than typical dianthus and a sweet, spicy clove fragrance, set above compact silvery-blue foliage. It blooms in flushes from early summer through fall, especially with deadheading, and shows the improved heat tolerance and repeat flowering bred into the Fruit Punch series. Give it sharp drainage and let the soil dry slightly between waterings, since it resents constantly wet feet.

common_name: EverLast Orchid Dianthus (Proven Winners Fragrant Bubblegum-Pink Reblooming Interspecific Pink)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring or fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; EverLast Orchid is part of the Proven Winners EverLast series bred for a strong spring flush with reliable rebloom in fall.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. EverLast Orchid bears fragrant, bright bubblegum-pink double flowers with fringed petal edges held above a tidy mound of blue-green foliage, flushing heavily in spring, blooming through summer, and flushing again in fall. Though hardy as a perennial, it flowers so quickly from a young plant that growers also use it as a first-year bedding annual. Deadhead spent stems to keep new buds forming and avoid heavy, poorly drained soils that invite crown rot.

common_name: EverLast Lavender+Eye Dianthus (Proven Winners Fragrant Red-Eyed Reblooming Interspecific Pink)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring or fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; part of the Proven Winners EverLast series bred for a strong spring flush with reliable rebloom in fall.

directions: Plant container-grown divisions in spring or fall in lean, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. EverLast Lavender+Eye produces fragrant, double, soft lavender-pink flowers with a contrasting red eye and frilled petal edges over a compact mat of dark green, hairy-leaved foliage, blooming first in late spring and again in fall when deadheaded. It is more mat-forming than some EverLast siblings, making it useful as a small-scale groundcover or edging plant along a sunny border. Keep soil on the dry side between waterings, since standing moisture quickly leads to crown or root rot.

common_name: Jolt Cherry Dianthus (Heat-Tolerant Bedding Interspecific Pink with Red-Centered Cherry Blooms)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and set out transplants after frost danger has passed; Jolt Cherry is bred for exceptional heat tolerance and keeps flowering through the hottest part of summer.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into well-drained soil with a near-neutral pH in full sun once frost danger has passed. Jolt Cherry produces large, showy umbels of cherry-red florets that mature to pink with a darker red center, carried above fine, dark green foliage on sturdy stems that resist flopping in summer storms. It is among the most heat-tolerant garden dianthus available, continuing to bloom strongly through midsummer heat that stalls many other pinks, and flowers from late spring until frost. Deadhead spent umbels occasionally to keep new buds coming, and avoid overly rich soil that produces excess foliage at the expense of bloom.

common_name: Jolt Purple Dianthus (Heat-Tolerant Bedding Interspecific Pink with Vivid Purple-Pink Blooms)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost and set out transplants after frost danger has passed; Jolt Purple shares the series' exceptional heat tolerance and continues flowering through summer heat.

directions: Start seed indoors and transplant into well-drained, near-neutral soil in full sun once frost danger has passed. Jolt Purple carries luminous, frilly-edged florets in a vivid purple-pink with deeper purple overtones, held in large rounded umbels above a compact mound of fine dark green foliage on strong, weather-resistant stems. Like its Jolt series siblings it tolerates summer heat unusually well for a dianthus, blooming steadily from late spring through frost rather than stalling in midsummer. Deadhead spent umbels occasionally to encourage continued flowering, and avoid soggy or overly fertile soil, which weakens stems and reduces flower quality.
